activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Peyton ran to the park with Dad. She wanted to find her red ball. It was lost somewhere in the grass.

Peyton used her eyes to see. She saw swings. She saw a black dog. "No ball," she said. She used her ears to listen. She heard a squeak, squeak, squeak. The swings went up and down. Still no ball.

Then Peyton used her nose. She sniffed the air. She smelled popcorn! Dad said, "Let's look near the popcorn cart." Peyton used her hands to touch the grass. It felt soft and tickly. Her fingers found something round. "My ball!" she shouted. She hugged it. Dad gave her cold popcorn to taste. Mmm, it was salty. Peyton laughed. "Eyes, ears, nose, hands, tongue. I found it all!" The black dog wagged its tail.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Maeva went to the store with Mama. Near the apples there was a little red box. It was full of books. "One, two, three books," said Maeva, tapping each one. The top book had a fish on it. Blue fish. They could swim in deep, deep water. Maeva wanted that book. She wanted to keep it forever.

Mama pointed at the front of the book. There were little marks there. Words. "Those marks say the name," said Mama. Maeva traced them with her finger. Then she opened the book at the front, where the story begins. Page one. Page two. Page three. The fish swam and swam.

"You can take it home," said Mama. "But we bring it back soon. Then someone else can read it too." Maeva hugged the book to her chest. She sniffed the pages. They smelled like paper and apples. At home, she turned every page, one by one, all the way to the back. The very last page had a big fish. It looked right at her. "Hello, fish," said Maeva.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Athena had a little bunny toy. She brought it to daycare. But now bunny was gone.

Athena looked in the toy box. No bunny. She looked under the table. No bunny. Her friend Mia helped her look too.

It was winter, so snack was inside today. The teacher cut apples into slices. They were crunchy and good. Athena ate her snack. Then she looked some more.

Mia pulled a big rug back to sweep. The rug moved. And there was bunny! The rug had been hiding bunny all along. Athena picked bunny up and hugged him tight.

"Thank you, Mia," said Athena.

"Let's put bunny in your cubby next time," said Mia.

Athena smiled. She put bunny in her pocket, where he could not hide. Then she and Mia went to build a big tower of blocks together.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Isaiah held Mama's hand at the store. "Let's find your juice," said Mama. Isaiah loved juice. He wanted it fast!

First they passed the toy aisle. Isaiah saw a red ball and a little drum. He tapped the drum. Boom! It made a big sound. He laughed.

Next they passed the pet aisle. A puppy barked. Woof, woof! A fish swam in a small tank. Isaiah waved at the fish. The fish swam away fast.

Then Mama turned down a new aisle. It was full of food. Apples, bread, and milk! And there, on a long shelf, was the juice. Isaiah grabbed a box. It was apple juice, his favorite!

But wait. The cart had a toy duck in it. Isaiah did not put it there. He quacked, and Mama laughed. "Silly duck wants juice too," she said.

At home, Mama poured juice into Isaiah's cup. He drank it all up. "More juice, Mama! Please!"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Amira showed her the backyard. "This is my swing," said Amira. "This is my sand box. And these are my flowers."

The flowers were droopy. Their heads hung down low. "Oh dear," said Grandma. "They look sad." Amira wondered why. Had they lost their sun? Were they too hot?

Grandma filled the watering can at the tap. Amira helped hold the handle. They poured water on the dirt, one flower, two flowers, three flowers, four. The water sank down into the soil. It went slip, slip, slip.

The next morning, Amira ran outside. She stopped and stared. The flowers were standing up tall! Their heads were high, not low. "Grandma, come see!" she called.

Grandma came out with her warm sweater on. She sat in the sun and smiled. "The water helped them," said Grandma. "They drank it all up."

Amira patted the dirt around the roots. "I will keep you watered," she told the flowers. She counted them again. One, two, three, four. All tall.

Then she ran to the porch. She picked up her woolly toy sheep and held it out. "Grandma, my sheep is thirsty too," she said. "Can sheep drink from a cup?"

story:

"Mom, can you help me, please?" Leah asked. Mom reached back with one hand. She got the teddy bear. "Thank you, Mom," Leah said. Mom smiled at her in the mirror.

Then Leah sang a song. "One bear, one girl, one long car ride," she sang. Dad laughed at her joke. At a stop, Dad handed Leah a juice box. "Thank you," she said. She took a big sip. Oops. A drop fell on the seat. "Sorry, Dad," Leah said. "That is okay," said Dad. He wiped it with a napkin. The car went on. Leah hugged her bear and watched the trees swing by the window. "Home soon," said Mom.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Owen wanted the red truck. But Max had the red truck. Max was playing with it by the blocks.

Owen grabbed at the truck. The truck fell. It hit Max's foot. Max began to cry.

"Sorry, Max," said Owen. Miss Ali came over. "You can ask for help," she said. Owen took a big breath. "Can I have a turn, please?" he asked.

Max sniffed. He held out the truck. "Okay. Your turn."

"Thank you," said Owen. He pushed the truck across the carpet. Vroom! It went far under the windy-day picture on the wall.

Then Max whispered, "It is my birthday on Friday." Owen smiled. "Then you go first with the truck," he said.

Max clapped. The two boys sat side by side. The red truck went back and forth, back and forth, all morning long.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Mya stood at the school gate. The gate was huge and red. Mya did not want to let go of Papa's hand.

A big yellow bus stopped by the gate. The door opened with a hiss. Out came a girl with two braids. The girl waved at the bus. The bus door waved back, kind of, and then the bus drove away.

"Where did the bus go?" Mya asked.

"Home," said the girl with braids. "It comes back. We just have to wait."

Mya held the gate with one hand. She waited. She counted the cars that passed. One car. Two cars. Three cars. Then the bell rang, and the gate opened by itself.

"Look, Papa! I held the gate, and now it moves!"

"That's the magic of school," said Papa. "Every morning, the gate opens."

Inside, Mya saw a picture of a horse on the wall. A teacher smiled and said, "Hello, Mya. Come see our class horse. His name is Sam."

Mya looked back at the gate. Papa waved. Mya waved too, and then she ran to the horse. "Does Sam like to wait?" she asked.

"He waits for you every day," said the teacher.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Ryan ran into the music studio. "I want to play the drum!" he said. Miss Kim smiled. She put a big drum in front of him. Ryan hit it with the drumstick. Nothing happened. The drum made no sound at all.

"Why is it quiet?" Ryan asked. Miss Kim said, "Look at the drum top." Ryan looked. The drum top was soft and loose. It looked like a saggy blanket. "Can we fix it?" he asked. Miss Kim turned a little knob on the side. She passed the drumstick back to Ryan.

Ryan hit the drum again. BOOM! The drum top was tight now. Tight drum, big sound. Ryan hit it fast. Boom, boom, boom! His tummy jumped with the beat. Miss Kim clapped. Ryan felt very proud. "Again!" he shouted. Boom! Boom! Boom!

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zayn was a small boy on a big trip. He was in a hotel room with Mama and Baba. His toy bunny was missing. "Where is Bunny?" he asked.

Zayn looked under the bed. No Bunny. He looked near the chair. No Bunny. " Bunny likes to hide," said Mama with a smile. "Bunny is silly," said Zayn.

Then Zayn saw the curtains. They went all the way to the floor. He slid the curtain to one side. Bunny was there! "I found you!" said Zayn. The curtain had made a hiding spot. Now Zayn knew a trick. He slid the other curtain too. No bunny there, just his shoe. "My shoe was hiding too!" said Zayn. Mama laughed and laughed. Baba put Bunny on the pillow. "Sleep tight, Bunny," said Zayn. Bunny slid down the pillow, soft and slow.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Arnaud put on his pajamas. He was happy because tonight he had his favorite toy, a soft brown cow. He hugged the cow tight.

Dad turned on the little night light. It made a warm yellow glow. Then Dad said, "Look at the wall." A big dark shape sat there. It had long ears. Arnaud did not know what it was. His tummy felt tight. He was scared. He pulled his blanket up to his chin.

"That is my hand," said Dad. Dad held his hand near the light. The shape on the wall moved its ears. It was only a shadow! Arnaud laughed out loud. Dad helped Arnaud put his hand near the light too. A small shadow grew on the wall. Arnaud opened and closed his fingers. The shadow wiggled. He felt so excited. He made a dog shadow. Then he made a bird shadow with two hands.

Then Arnaud made a sad face. He wanted a cow shadow, but his hands would not make one. "Too hard," he said. His mouth turned down. Dad sat on the bed. "Make a point with your fingers," said Dad. Arnaud tried. He made two little horns on top. "Moo!" he shouted. Now it was a cow shadow.

Dad turned the big light off. The yellow glow stayed on. Arnaud held his cow close to his chest. His eyes got heavy. He yawned one big yawn. Dad kissed his head and said, "Time to sleep." Arnaud closed his eyes. The little shadow hand on the wall waved good night.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Yesterday, Evelyn found a big puddle at the park. She splashed in it with her red boots. The water went splash, splash, splash.

Today the puddle was little. "Oh no," said Evelyn. "My puddle is small." Mama sat on the wide bench nearby. "The sun is out now," Mama said. "The sun makes wet things dry."

Evelyn watched the sun shine on the puddle. She sat down. She waited. She looked at a bird. She looked at the sky.

Later, the puddle was just a dark spot on the ground. Evelyn stomped her boot. It did not splash. It went tap.

"Come back tomorrow," Evelyn said to the spot. "Maybe it will rain again."

Mama laughed softly. "Maybe it will," she said. "And you can bring your boots."

Evelyn held her boots in her hands. She gave the empty spot a big pat, like a present for tomorrow.

"Bye bye, puddle," she said.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Jules ran to the community garden with a little shovel. He wanted to grow big carrots. His grandma helped him dig the soil. Jules dropped the tiny seeds into the dark dirt. Then he patted them down, pat, pat, pat.

Every day Jules came back to look. Nothing grew. Nothing at all! Jules felt worried. "Where are my carrots?" he asked. Grandma pointed at the sky. "No rain," she said. "Seeds need water to grow." Jules got his small watering can. He poured water on the dirt. Splash, splash, splash.

The next day, something green peeked out! Tiny leaves! "It grew!" Jules shouted. He watered the leaves every day. Soon the leaves grew tall and bushy. Then Jules saw a surprise. A green frog sat under the leaves! The frog hopped away, hop, hop, hop.

At last, grandma pulled up the carrots. They were big and red! Jules held one up high. "Look what water made grow!" he said. Grandma laughed and clapped her hands. "Carrots for dinner," she said. Jules hugged his red carrot tight.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. It was her first haircut. The chair was too tall, so Mama lifted her up.

The hairdresser wore a shiny key on her belt. Beatrice liked to watch it swing. The hairdresser put a cape on Beatrice. The cape was not bad at all. It felt soft.

Then the hairdresser picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. It stuck there, like a small brown line.

Beatrice pointed. "It stays!" she said.

"It sticks to the cape," said the hairdresser. "Want to see more fall?"

Beatrice nodded. Snip, snip. More hair fell. More little lines stuck to her lap. She counted them with one finger.

"Pretty," said Beatrice.

Then the hairdresser brushed the cape. All the little lines slid off, one by one. Beatrice watched every one fall to the floor.

"My turn is done," said the hairdresser. "Look in the mirror."

Beatrice looked. Her hair was short and smooth. She smiled at the girl in the glass, and the girl smiled back.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Elijah went to the store with his mom. In the corner was a little library shelf. Elijah found a book about a cute puppy. The cover had words on it. "That says puppy," said Mom. Elijah pointed at the words. Then he opened the book. He turned the pages one by one. First page, then the next, all the way to the end. "It goes front to back," he said.

Elijah held the book tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. Mom shook her head. "We borrow it," she said. "We take it home. Then we bring it back on the due day." A lady at the desk stamped a paper. Elijah looked at the stamp. "So other kids can read it too," said Mom.

At home, Elijah read the puppy book two times. He skip-skipped to his room with it. That night he dreamed about the puppy. In the morning he said, "We take it back on the big day." Mom smiled. "Yes," she said. "And then we can borrow one more."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Leah wanted to find the letter S in class. It was hiding from her. She looked on the big chart. She looked on the door. No S anywhere.

Teacher Mia held up a card. "What sound does this one make?" The card had a curvy letter on it. "S goes sssss," said Teacher Mia, like a snake.

Then Leah heard it. Sun. Sun began with ssss! She whispered, "Ssss, sun." Her friend Ben laughed. "You sound like a leaky tire," he said. Leah laughed too. "Ssss, snake. Ssss, sock. Ssss, Ben!" Ben put his hands on his ears. "Not me! I start with B!"

The hard part was the curvy shape. Leah drew an S on her paper. It slipped and looked like a wiggly worm. Ben said, "That is a sleepy S." Leah tried again. Slow and curvy. There it was.

She ran to the rug and picked up her sun toy. "This starts with S," she said. "Ssss, sun." Teacher Mia gave her a star sticker. Leah stuck it on her paper, right next to the wiggly worm.

story:
Abigail was at Grandma's house. She wanted to paint a big green hill. But Grandma had no green paint.

Grandma set out the paints. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. No green anywhere.

"Where did the green go?" Abigail wondered.

She dipped her brush in blue. She made a blue hill. Then she dipped in yellow. She painted yellow on top of the blue hill.

The hill turned green!

"Look, Grandma!" said Abigail. "Blue and yellow made green!"

Grandna smiled. "Try red and yellow too," she said.

Abigail mixed red and yellow. It made orange, like a pumpkin.

After all that painting, Abigail gave a big yawn. The friendly old cat curled up beside her. Together they watched the sun go down over the green hill.

"Blue and yellow," Abigail whispered. "Green."

story:
Elena was at Grandma's house. She wanted to feed the fish in the pond. The fish were big and orange. They liked to swim near the little bridge.

Elena could not find the fish food. The jar was too high on a shelf. She tried to reach it. Grandma said, "Stop, that is not safe. Ask me for help." Elena said, "Please, Grandma, can you help me?" Grandma smiled. She got the jar down with a long grabber tool. "Thank you," said Elena.

Elena ran to the pond. She was so happy, the jar slipped. It fell in the wet grass. Some food spilled out. "Sorry, Grandma," said Elena. "That is okay," said Grandma. "The grass likes it too."

Then they sprinkled the food together. The fish came fast. Their tails splashed. Elena felt the cool air on her face. "It is getting late," said Grandma. "One more handful, then we go in." Elena threw the food. The fish gobbled it up. Grandma held her hand as they walked to the door.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Kinsley sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. She was going to Grandma's house. Yesterday, Kinsley picked peaches with Grandma. The peaches were big and juicy. One fell off the tree when she pulled it. Now the peaches sat in a basket on the seat.

"Are we there now?" Kinsley asked. "Not yet," said Mommy. "We will get there soon." Kinsley looked out the window. A big truck went by. Then a cow went by. Then the cow was gone. It was behind them now.

Kinsley held her book. She turned the pages one by one. The sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on her shoe. She moved her foot. The warm spot moved too. She put her foot back. The warm spot came back. Kinsley laughed.

The car stopped. "Here we are," said Mommy. Grandma stood by the door. She had flour on her hands. "We will bake a peach pie today," said Grandma. "And tomorrow, we will eat it." Kinsley climbed down from the car seat. She carried the basket with both hands. "I picked these yesterday," she said. Grandma smiled and opened the door wide.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Henry was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose was stuffy. He wanted to play outside. But the sky was cloudy. Grandma said, "Rest today."

Henry sat at the table. He felt grumpy. Grandma made him warm soup. She stirred the big pot. The pot made steam. Little white puffs floated up.

Henry leaned over his bowl. The warm steam touched his face. He sniffed. His nose felt better. He sniffed again. It opened up. "I can smell it!" he said.

He ate the soup slowly. More steam rose. More sniffs came. His nose was all clear now. Grandma smiled. "You want more?" she asked. Henry nodded. She ladled a second bowl from the pot.

"Tomorrow we can go to the store," Grandma said. "When your nose is all better." Henry blew on his spoon. The steam curled up. He watched it go. "More steam, please," he said.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Jules had a runny nose today. He had to stay home. Mama said his body needed rest.

Jules wanted to see out the window. But the window was all white. He could not see the birds.

In the kitchen, Mama filled a big pot. She put it on the stove. Mama kept Jules far from the hot stove. He stood by the table.

The pot went plop, plop, plop. Steam rose up. The steam floated high. It went all the way to the window.

Jules looked at the window. The white got wet. Then his finger made a line in it. He drew a big heart. He drew a sun too.

The window opened a little bit. Cool air came in. Slowly, the heart went away. The sun went away too.

Jules waited. More steam came up. The window turned white again. He drew the heart one more time.

Papa came in with soup. "Is that my heart on the window?" he asked.

"That one is for you," said Jules. He drew a little heart next to it.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Harper ran to the fence. The sheep were waiting there.

"I want to learn my senses today," she said. Grandma smiled. "Then let's go!"

First Harper peeked at a sheep. "I see it with my eyes!" she said. The sheep was white and fluffy.

Next she heard a loud "Baa!" She covered her ears. "My ears heard that!"

Harper touched the sheep's soft wool. "My hands feel it," she said. "So soft!"

Grandma picked an apple. Harper smelled it. "My nose smells it. Yum!"

Then Grandma cut the apple with her knife. She gave Harper a small piece. Harper tasted it. "My mouth tastes it! Sweet!"

Harper jumped up and down. "Eyes, ears, hands, nose, mouth!" she said. "I know all five!"

The sheep went "Baa!" again, loud and long.

"Even you know that was right," Harper said.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Layla woke up at Grandma's house. It was a sunny morning. She wanted to help Grandma make bread. Grandma said, "First we use our hands." Layla patted the soft dough. "Hands feel!" said Layla. "That is touch," said Grandma. "One."

Then Grandma put the bread in the oven. Grandma did that part, because the oven was hot. Layla watched from her chair. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet. Layla sniffed with her nose. "Nose smells!" said Layla. "That is smell," said Grandma. "Two."

The bread came out. Grandma cut one slice. Layla took a bite. "My tongue tastes it!" said Layla. "Yum. That is taste. Three." Grandma rang a little bell. Layla's ears heard it. "Ears hear! Four," she said. Then Layla looked at her favorite slice, still warm. "My eyes see it! Five!" Grandma laughed. "All five," said Grandma. Layla counted on her fingers, one by one. "Hands, nose, tongue, ears, eyes." Then she took another big bite.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a cold. His nose was red and his sock feet were warm under a blanket.

Mom brought him a cup of warm water with honey. Steam rose up from the cup. "Look at the steam, Arthur," said Mom. "What does it do?" The little cloud floated up. Then it went away. Arthur breathed in. The warm air felt soft in his nose. His nose opened up! He could smell Mom's soup in the kitchen.

Arthur took another breath. Where did the steam go now? It went up to the ceiling. It did not come back down. The cup got cooler in his hands. When the steam went away, the water was not hot anymore.

Arthur sniffed the air. "Soup!" he said. "I can smell it again." His tummy made a little growl. Mom smiled. "More warm water first," she said. Arthur held the cup. New steam curled up, up, up. He watched it all the way to the ceiling.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Oliver was at Grandma's house. The big game was on TV. Everyone wanted snacks, but the popcorn bowl was empty.

Grandpa said he would make more. Oliver watched from his chair. Grandpa put kernels in a pot. Then he turned on the stove. "You stay back, buddy," Grandpa said. Oliver stayed back.

Soon the pot went pop, pop, pop. Each pop made a white puff jump up. The puffs filled the pot. Then the puffs filled the big blue bowl.

Oliver clapped his hands. The pops had made the bowl full again! Grandpa carried the bowl to the couch. Everyone took a handful.

Oliver ate one puff. It was warm and salty. "More pops, more popcorn," said Oliver. Grandpa laughed and pointed at the pot.

"Want to watch it pop again?"

"Yes," said Oliver. "I will not blink."

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Victor was three today. Grandma and Grandpa came. So did his friend Sam.

On the table was a big cake. On the cake were three little candles. Daddy lit them with a match. Daddy held the match far from Victor.

The candles made small flames. They jumped and wiggled.

"Are the flames scary?" asked Victor.

"No," said Mommy. "They are small. And we blow them out."

Victor chose to blow. He took a big breath. He blew hard.

The flames went out. All three! Smoke curled up like little gray ribbons.

Victor laughed. "I did that!"

Then Sam wanted a turn. But the candles were already out. So Mommy put one new candle on a cupcake. Sam blew, and that flame went out too.

Everybody clapped. "Happy birthday, Victor!" they said.

Victor blew a kiss to the smoke.

story:
Brielle stood in the gym with her class. Miss Kay, a kind woman with a big smile, put a hoop on the floor. "Watch me," she said. She tossed a beanbag. It landed in the hoop. Everyone clapped.

Now it was Brielle's turn. She held the beanbag in her hand. She threw it. The beanbag flew far. It landed past the hoop. "Oh no," said Brielle. Leo threw his next. His beanbag missed too. Leo made an angry face and stamped his foot. Miss Kay knelt down. "Try again," she said softly. "Just a little throw." She moved close and held out her hand near the hoop.

Brielle looked at Miss Kay's hand. She tossed the beanbag soft and low. It went in! "I did it!" said Brielle. Leo tried a little throw too. His beanbag went in. "Good throw, Leo!" said Brielle. Leo smiled big.

Then Miss Kay rolled a big ball to Brielle. The ball hit her chest and fell down. It rolled away. "Hold out both arms," said Miss Kay. Brielle held out both arms like a big hug. Miss Kay rolled the ball again. Brielle squeezed it with both hands. She caught it!

"Again!" said Brielle. Miss Kay rolled the ball. Brielle caught it and hugged it tight. Leo clapped for her. Then Brielle rolled the ball gently to Leo.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Natalie was on the Bunny team. All the players had to wear red shirts. Natalie was shy at the first game. She stood still and did not kick the ball.

At practice, Coach Kim said, "Try a big kick, Natalie." Natalie kicked the ball soft. The ball rolled a little bit. Then she kicked it hard. The ball went far, all the way to the net. "Whoa," said Natalie. A big kick made the ball go far.

The next game, Natalie ran to the ball. She saw a little ant on the grass. She stepped over it. Then she took her kick. The ball flew across the field. Her friend Maya caught it and kicked it too. "Nice kick!" Maya called.

The other team got the ball. Maya felt sad. Natalie patted her back. "You can try again," Natalie said. Maya smiled.

Near the end of the game, the ball came to Natalie one more time. She looked at the net. She pulled her leg back and kicked with all her might. The ball went in! The Bunnies cheered. Natalie jumped up and down with Maya. "We did it!" said Natalie.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Maya stood in the school hallway. Her mama held her hand. Maya saw a row of little hooks on the wall. Each hook held a backpack. But one hook was empty. "That one is for you," said Mama.

Maya reached up. She hung her backpack on the empty hook. She let go. The backpack stayed put. Maya smiled. The hook held her bag, just like the others.

A teacher came to the door. "Come see the sand table," she said. Maya ran to it. She pushed her hands into the cool sand. The sand ran between her fingers.

Then Mama waved. "Bye, Maya. I will be back soon." Maya did not cry. She knew the hook would keep her backpack safe. She knew Mama would come back too.

She filled a red cup with sand. Then she tipped it over. "Look, teacher!" said Maya. "I caught the sand in my hand."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Natalie sat at the paint table at daycare. She wanted to paint a big green frog. But there was no green paint. She looked in the cups. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. She asked her teacher, "Where is the green?"

"You can find out," said the teacher.

Natalie dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She made a yellow frog on her paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She brushed it over the yellow frog. The yellow frog turned green! Natalie clapped her hands. Her hands were messy with paint.

The sun did shine in the window. It made the green frog glow on the paper. Then Mia came over with a red knee. The doctor had given her a bandage. Natalie pointed at it. "My frog has red eyes too," she said. She dipped a clean brush in the red paint. She added two red eyes. "There," said Natalie. "Hello, green frog."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Jack stood at the airport with Mama. He wanted to see Grandma first. "Look for a blue coat," Mama said. Jack watched the big doors. One, two, three people walked out. Then a blue coat came too. "Grandma!" Jack shouted. Grandma hugged him tight.

Grandma had one big bag and one small bag. Jack pulled the small bag on its wheels. The bag was heavy, so it rolled slow. Then Jack pulled it on the smooth floor, and it rolled fast. "Like an ant carrying a big leaf," Grandma said with a laugh. The young helper smiled.

At home, Grandma unpacked her things. "Here is a gift," she said. It was a soft teddy bear. Jack hugged the bear. "Will you stay a long time?" he asked. "A whole week," said Grandma. "One whole week with you."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Wesley stood by the fish tanks at the pet store. He saw a little gold fish swimming in a circle. "I want that one," said Wesley. His mom smiled. "That one can be yours."

At home, Mom helped him set up a small tank. Wesley poured the water. The fish swam fast in its new home. Then the fish bumped the glass. It swam to the top. It bumped again. Wesley felt worried. "Is he hungry?"

Mom got the tiny food can. Wesley dropped one small pinch in. The fish swam up fast. It opened its little mouth. Gulp, gulp. The food was gone. "He was hungry," said Wesley. He clapped his hands.

Now Wesley feeds the fish each morning with Mom. He taps the tall tank gently. The fish swims over in a circle to say hello. "Good morning, little fish," says Wesley. The fish blows a tiny bubble.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Mateo sat on a soft red rug at the library. He wanted to find a book about turtles. But he could not read the letters yet.

A girl sat next to him. She had a thick book full of letters. "This is M," she said. "It says mmm, like milk." Mateo patted the letter. "Mmm," he said. "M is for Mateo."

Then he looked at the shelves. He found a sign with M on it. "Mmm, mmm," he said. The sign said MICE. He pulled out a book. The cover had a little mouse on it. He opened it. It was a mouse book, not a turtle book.

"Almost," said the girl. "Try T. T says tuh, like top." Mateo walked slowly along the shelf. He waited. He looked at each sign. Then he saw it. A big red T. "Tuh," he said. "T is for turtle!" He pulled the book out. A green turtle smiled at him from the cover.

Mateo sat back on the rug. He put his hand on the cover. "Tuh, tuh, turtle," he said softly. The girl clapped. "You found it," she said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Violet went to the library with her mom. The room smelled like paper. It was quiet. Violet heard pages turning.

She found a book with a red boat on the front. She wanted to keep it forever. "Can I take it home?" she asked.

The librarian gave her a little card. "You can borrow the boat book," she said. "Bring it back soon, so other kids can read it too."

Violet held the book tight. She did not want to share it. She tried to hide it under her coat. Mom saw her. "The book has to go back," Mom said softly. "But we can come again."

At home, Violet opened the book. She turned the pages from the front. On each page, words sat in rows. Mom pointed at the words. "These tell the story," she said. Mom read them out loud. The words made the boat sail in Violet's mind.

Soon it was time to go back. The book shelf looked empty without the red boat book. Violet gave it to the librarian. Then she found a new one. "This one," she said, holding it up high.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Wesley came to school early. He saw his teacher, Miss Kim, at the play table. She had a big box. "What is in the box?" Wesley asked. "Open it and see," said Miss Kim.

Wesley used his hands to open it. Inside were little cups. He picked one up. He sniffed it with his nose. It smelled like oranges. He put it near his mouth. He took a tiny taste with his tongue. It was sweet. "It is orange juice?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Kim. "You found out with your nose and your tongue."

Then Wesley heard a shout. Miss Kim shouted, "Look out!" A tower of wood blocks fell over. It made a big sound in his ears. Wesley looked with his eyes. His friend Tom had pushed it. The blocks were all over the floor.

But there was a surprise inside the tower. A little red car was hiding there. It rolled right to Wesley's feet. Wesley touched it with his fingers. It was smooth and cool. "Vroom," said Wesley. He smiled. "Can I keep it?" Tom laughed and said, "It is yours now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Sienna sat in the car seat. Her bunny was not in her lap. "Where is Bunny?" she asked. Mom looked in the mirror. "Let us look together," said Mom.

Sienna looked down by her feet. She saw a shoe. She saw a cracker. No bunny. She looked under her coat. No bunny. Her tummy felt tight. "I want Bunny," she said.

Mom stopped the car in the driveway. She turned on the lamp above Sienna's head. The warm light made the seat bright. Now Sienna could see into the dark corner. There was Bunny, wedged under the brown strap. "Bunny!" said Sienna. She pulled Bunny out and hugged him soft.

Mom helped Sienna out of the car. Sienna held Bunny close. "Thank you, Mom," she said. "The lamp helped me see." Mom smiled and kissed her head. They walked to the door, hand in hand.

Inside, Sienna put Bunny on the pillow. She patted his ears. "Bunny can rest now," she said. "You too," said Mom, and she tucked them both in.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Thomas was at Grandma's house for the party. Everyone was singing songs for the holiday. Thomas wanted to hold a candle like the big kids.

"You are too small for fire," said Auntie May. "Here is your own special light." She gave him a little lamp with a switch.

Thomas pressed the switch. The lamp glowed. He pressed it again. The lamp went dark. "Look, Grandma! I can make night and morning!"

Grandma laughed. "You are the sun now, Thomas." Thomas made the light blink on and off. His baby cousin clapped her hands each time.

Later, they all walked down the street with their candles. It was getting late. Thomas held his lamp up high. Every time he pressed the switch, his shadow jumped on the wall.

"I have a dancing shadow!" said Thomas. "On, off, on, off!" His shadow grew tall, then small, then tall again. "Best lamp ever," he whispered to it.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Stella woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! The sky had been stormy last night. Now school was closed. It was a snow day at home.

Stella ran to the backyard. She wanted to slide down the little hill. But her sled was in the shed. The shed door was stuck. Dad pulled and pulled. It would not open.

Then Stella saw the big snow pile by the fence. She pushed it with her mittens. The snow moved! She pushed again. A big ball rolled away. "Look, Dad! My hands make it go!"

They rolled three big balls. Stella stacked them up. Dad put on a carrot nose. "It's a snow cow!" said Dad. "Moo," said Stella. She touched its cold, lumpy back. The snow cow smiled all morning.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story: Theodore stood in the school yard. His teacher Miss Ann held out a hoop. "Try to toss the beanbag in," she said. Theodore squeezed his hat under one arm. He tossed the beanbag. It hit the edge and fell out. He frowned. His friend Ben's beanbag went in. Ben stood close to the hoop. Theodore saw that. He took two steps closer. He tossed again. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. It landed in the hoop. "It went in!" said Theodore. Then Miss Ann rolled him a big ball. It bumped his chest and fell. He tried one hand. It fell again. He held out both arms. Miss Ann rolled the ball. It landed soft in his hands, like a big crunchy apple. "I caught it!" he said. Miss Ann clapped.
